in_scope.title: Site Isolation is Dead: How Site Isolation is Broken in Agentic Browsers and Extensions
in_scope.title_norm: site isolation is dead how site isolation is broken in agentic browsers and extensions
in_scope.grounding: full-text (author-hosted S&P'26 PDF, open access). Read in full: abstract, S1, S2/S2.1 incl. Table 1, S4 (S4.1 MPI + Table 2, S4.3 scenarios, S4.4 feasibility study), S5 preamble + S5.1 opening, S5.4 guardrail design/evaluation incl. Table 3, S6 Discussion. NOT read line-by-line: S3 threat model, S4.2 SLI mechanism, S5.2, S5.3, S7 related work, S8, Appendix Tables 4-7. NOTE: the word 'Electron' NEVER appears in the paper (grep-confirmed) - targets are Chromium-based agentic browsers (BrowserOS, Vibe) and 7 Chrome extensions. ADJACENT tag reflects that the vulnerability class - a privileged process accepting forged IPC from a compromised renderer with no origin check - is structurally identical to Electron's renderer<->main / ipcMain trust problem, but the paper makes no Electron claim. Table 2 per-cell values were read as flattened PDF text and reconstructed from S4.1 prose; re-verify before quoting individual cells.
in_scope.why_it_matters: Closest thing in the ledger to a published, end-to-end demonstration that renderer->privileged-process IPC trust failure defeats process isolation in a real desktop application family. Key numbers: 9 systems analyzed (2 open-source agentic browsers + 7 Chrome extensions), ALL vulnerable to MPI and/or SLI; WebPilot the only MPI-immune one, and only because it exposes no risky actions. Renderer RCE chained from CVE-2025-0291 + Chromium Issue 379140430 on Chromium 130.0.6723.160, then forged Mojo IPC at the C++ level - site isolation bypassed WITHOUT an additional sandbox escape. Guardrail: IPI ASR 0.89 -> 0.00 (BrowserOS) and 0.52 -> 0.00 (Nanobrowser), TSR 0.20 -> 0.14 and 0.27 -> 0.29 on 100 WebArena tasks.

in_scope.title: From Documentation to Zero-day Vulnerabilities: LLM-Driven Fuzzing of JavaScript Engines in PDF Readers
in_scope.title_norm: from documentation to zero-day vulnerabilities llm-driven fuzzing of javascript engines in pdf readers
in_scope.grounding: FULL-TEXT as of 2026-08-23. arXiv:2608.06641v2 (18 Aug 2026) PDF fetched successfully (103,792 chars / 1,616 lines) and read end-to-end: abstract, S1-S10, Tables 1-4, Listings 1-5, Figure 1 caption. v2 is the CAMERA-READY and carries the ACM DOI 10.1145/3830454.3832609 and ISBN 979-8-4007-2871-6/2026/11 in the copyright block - this supersedes yesterday's 'ACM DOI not yet assigned'. Provenance recipe that worked: WebSearch the paper TITLE -> fetch arxiv.org/abs/... (which places the /pdf/ URL in the provenance set) -> fetch arxiv.org/pdf/... . A direct /pdf/ fetch as the first call is rejected ('URL not in provenance set'). STILL UNREAD/UNREADABLE: Figure 2 (six coverage curves; only axis ranges survive PDF-to-text flattening - no curve value may be quoted); Table 1 rows for IDs 10-14 and 26-28 are ELIDED as '...' in the extracted text, so eight vulnerabilities' per-ID type/impact/status are unavailable; the reference list was read only far enough to resolve the key citations.
in_scope.why_it_matters: Structurally the same target class as Electron - a native desktop application that embeds a JavaScript engine and exposes a large DOCUMENTED privileged host API to attacker-supplied script - and it turns the vendor's own API manual into both the grammar AND the inter-call constraint system that drives discovery. FULL-TEXT-GROUNDED numbers: targets Adobe Acrobat Reader v24.005.20421, Foxit PDF Reader v2024.4.0.27683, PDF-XChange Editor v10.5.2.395; DynamoRIO basic-block coverage, 5 independent 24h runs per tool per target; 2-week vulnerability campaign, crashes caught by werfault.exe, manually triaged; VM = 4 cores/8GB/Windows 8.1, crashes re-verified on Win10 22H2 + Win11 24H2. Coverage: up to 48% over Cooper (the source of the abstract's headline), 37% over TypeOracle, 19% over TypeOracle+Cooper, 17% over TypeOracle+Favocado, 15% over Favocado, 16-49% over Claude-3.7-Sonnet. Vulnerabilities: 57 crashing inputs (23 Adobe / 24 Foxit / 10 PDF-XChange) dedup by normalized call-stack signature to 31 unique zero-days; 11 potentially ACE; 26 of 31 fixed; 10 CVEs assigned; $2,450 bounty on TWO vulnerabilities (not on 26). THE KEY NUMBER FOR THIS THESIS: Table 1 aggregated row shows candidate-relationships-only finds 12 vulnerabilities while strong symbolic relationships find 28 and PDFuzzer-full 31 - i.e. co-occurrence is not enough, parameter-value constraints and ordering are what surface the bugs. Relationship distribution (Table 2, n=1,019): value-constraint 887 (87.0%), producer-consumer 69 (6.8%), implicit 63 (6.2%) - a producer-consumer-only model, the assumption behind most prior API fuzzers, misses ~93%. Instantiation success (Table 3, 71,586 invocations over 1,000 PDFs): 91.5% overall, value-constraint 95.1%, producer-consumer 81.5%, IMPLICIT ONLY 64.0%. Scale: 666 API functions / 886 parameters (435 documented fns + 507 params; 231 undocumented fns + 379 params); brute-force pair analysis would be 221,445 pairs x ~30s = >1,845 hours, hence the two-stage RAG design. LLM accuracy: spec inference 94% (82/87 params), grammar generation 97% APIs / 98% params, relationship inference 93% (56/60). Cost: $60.77 (GPT-4o) end-to-end vs $76.14-$174.83 for naive LLM; throughput ~3/s strong-relationship test cases, up to 20/s regular. LLM choice is near-irrelevant (<1% coverage difference on Adobe). The word 'Electron' NEVER appears in the full text (grep-confirmed, along with 'browser', 'Chromium', 'Node.js', 'desktop'); the Electron mapping is this watch's analysis. GAPS IT LEAVES OPEN for a discovery thesis: (1) single-process engine memory safety only - no cross-process propagation (Electron renderer->main IPC); (2) closed-source commercial targets force black-box fuzzing with DynamoRIO, whereas Electron app source usually sits readable inside the asar, leaving room for static+symbolic hybrid extraction; (3) a single fixed input source (the document file) - no multi-source problem of the kind Buzz to Boom's taxonomy describes; (4) the evaluation deliberately holds the fuzzing LOOP constant (TypeOracle's wrapper, no coverage-guided feedback) so it compares generators only and says nothing about feedback-driven fuzzers; (5) S8's 'generalization beyond PDF' is a FEASIBILITY STUDY ONLY - 2,925 Word VBA APIs / 3,768 parameters extracted from 5,920 pages of docs and CFGs built, but NO fuzzing run and no results. Best single hook for the thesis: implicit (state-mediated) relationships are the type this paper instantiates WORST (64.0%), and they are precisely the DOMINANT form of Electron IPC channel dependency (login -> session handle -> file access).

fulltext_notes_2026-08-18.mpv_definition_verbatim: S1: 'A noteworthy property of a Message Progression Vulnerability - differentiating it from existing ones - is the involvement of multiple Electron processes, leading to chaining two or more vulnerabilities through multi-step message passing, to the final consequence.' Prior message-related vulnerabilities 'only need at most one-step exploitation from one process to another.' This is the sharpest available statement of the gap the paper claims over the ledger's existing Electron corpus.
fulltext_notes_2026-08-18.gap_claim_against_prior_electron_work: S1: 'existing Electron security studies mainly focus on unsafe configuration checks, and mitigation of malicious Document Object Model (DOM) content, or unsafe cross-context communication. None of them detects the progression of attacker-controlled messages across multiple Electron processes, let alone MPV.' It further argues cross-context STATIC analyses 'struggle with the dynamic message construction and asynchronous message passing', and that existing DYNAMIC web fuzzers 'are monolithic and do not coordinate across Electron's process boundaries', wasting budget on 'inputs that fail to propagate past the first boundary'. Directly names the limitation of the config-auditing line (Inspectron) and the DOM line (NDSS'23 DOM-tree typing / COINDEF) that this ledger already holds in in_scope.
fulltext_notes_2026-08-18.motivating_example_paperlib: Figure 1 / S2.1, verbatim: a victim clicks a malicious 'paperlib://' URI embedded in a webpage (A), which triggers a chain of THREE vulnerabilities across Electron's processes via message passing - an unintended function invocation in the MAIN process (B), a client-side request forgery in the UTILITY process (C), and DOM-based XSS in the RENDERER (D) - ultimately yielding arbitrary command execution. Described as a 'four-step chain, spanning three Electron processes'. The CVE is redacted in the preprint as 'CVE-2025-XXXX'. Note the utility process: this is the only item in the whole ledger that treats Electron's UTILITY process as part of the attack surface.
fulltext_notes_2026-08-18.source_taxonomy_three_types: S2.2.2 defines exactly three payload sources, coded U/F/S in Table 1. (U) Custom URI - 'app://action?content=payload'; the OS invokes the Electron app and delivers the URI to its open-url handler. (S) Remote Server Response - attacker-controlled values flow to network APIs such as fetch; 'commonly arises when an intermediate vulnerability, such as a client-side request forgery (CSRF), happens', and 'commonly appears in applications supporting plugin installation, remote file loading, and MCP server imports'. (F) Local File Access - attacker-controlled values flow to fs.readFile or BrowserWindow.loadFile; verbatim: 'No prior file system compromise is required: an attacker can exploit browser auto-download to silently place a malicious file in the default downloads directory, then trigger a custom URI to cause the application to load it.' THESIS VALUE: this is a published, citable source taxonomy for Electron desktop apps, and it converges independently with the delivery channels this watch derived from vendor advisories (config/profile files, sync, export, LLM output) - both say the untrusted-input frontier of a desktop app is NOT the network request.
fulltext_notes_2026-08-18.sink_taxonomy_intermediate_vs_terminal: S2.2.3 + Table 1 caption, verbatim: 'intermediate sinks forward attacker-controlled data into a message destined for another process; terminal sinks directly cause the security consequence (e.g., OS command execution)', and 'a single API may act as either depending on the runtime context'. Intermediate sinks are also called Progression APIs and 'generalize the notion of message passing beyond explicit IPC' (S3), covering script execution, window navigation and custom protocol handlers, not just ipcRenderer/ipcMain. Conditionally-terminal APIs named: contents.executeJavaScript(T) and eval(T).
fulltext_notes_2026-08-18.process_model_verbatim: S2.2.1: main process runs Node.js with full native API access; UTILITY processes are 'spawned by the main to handle background tasks such as network requests and file access, and ALSO run with Node.js access'; renderers display web content. Under the default secure configuration each renderer keeps two isolated JS contexts - the preload context (privileged: process, ipcRenderer; exposes selectively via contextBridge) and the main-world context (standard browser APIs + whatever preload exposed).
fulltext_notes_2026-08-18.method_two_phases: Phase I: static progression analysis identifies candidate vulnerable paths and segment boundaries by reasoning about payload injection points, IPC message flows and dangerous API sinks. Phase II: coverage-guided fuzzing per segment with two objectives - reach a terminal sink in the current process, OR reach a Progression API that propagates the payload to the next process, in which case the produced message SEEDS THE CORPUS of the next segment. Halting per segment (S4.3): (i) terminal sink reached and PoC saved, (ii) branch coverage saturates with no new Progression API output for k iterations, or (iii) global time budget expires. Algorithm 1 also skips segments containing only INVERTIBLE operations and reconstructs their inputs afterwards by inversion.
fulltext_notes_2026-08-18.llm_role: LLMs are used as an AGENT inside the pipeline, not as the detector. Per S4.2 the agent must emit four artifacts per discovered path: (1) an analysis.md of sources/sinks/segment boundaries, (2) a dataflow-segments.json enumerating each segment with code location, process type and links to neighbours, (3) per-segment fuzzing harnesses, and (4) LLM-generated seeds for each segment's initial corpus (S4.3: 'one representative input per parse branch'). Appendix D (UNREAD) is titled 'Agent Design' with D.1 Taint Analysis and Segmentation Agent and D.2 Harness Synthesis Agent. The specific model name is NOT stated in the portion read.
fulltext_notes_2026-08-18.why_this_matters_to_the_thesis: This is now the best-grounded statement in the repo of the METHODOLOGICAL gap a discovery thesis can claim: config auditing (Inspectron) and DOM-content defenses (NDSS'23, COINDEF) are single-process and single-step; monolithic web fuzzers cannot cross Electron's process boundaries. It also supplies a ready-made vocabulary - sources U/F/S, Progression APIs, intermediate vs terminal sinks, segmentation boundaries - that a thesis can adopt or explicitly argue against. Caution: because it is arXiv-only it must be cited as a preprint, and S6's numbers should not be quoted until the evaluation section is actually read.

Most thesis-relevant, all landing squarely on the boundaries this thesis targets: (a) CONTEXT-ISOLATION BYPASSES — CVE-2026-70601 (7.5 HIGH, CWE-693): apps exposing Promise-returning functions via contextBridge (the standard wrapper for ipcRenderer.invoke) let untrusted web content hijack Function.prototype.bind and reach the isolated preload world and every capability it holds, escalating to Node.js access where the renderer is unsandboxed or nodeIntegration is on; CVE-2026-70610 (5.4 MEDIUM, CWE-1321): the contextBridge object-copy path used v8::Object::Set ([[Set]] semantics) in CreateProxyForAPI (shell/renderer/api/electron_api_context_bridge.cc), so a crafted __proto__ property fired the inherited Object.prototype setter and polluted the prototype of objects landing in the privileged preload context — fixed by switching to CreateDataProperty ([[DefineOwnProperty]]), PR #51083, fix commits 2026-04-16, GHSA-ff2p-hmqr-hxm4; CVE-2026-34780 (8.3 HIGH): context-isolation bypass via bridged WebCodecs VideoFrame objects. CVE-2026-70598.detail: In offscreen rendering mode the MAIN process does not validate that the byte count implied by the GPU-supplied frame geometry fits the received shared-memory buffer, so a compromised GPU process makes the main process read out-of-bounds while producing 'paint' event images - memory disclosure or crash. CVE-2026-34764.detail: The release() callback handed to app code on a 'paint' event texture can outlive its backing native state; invoking it afterwards dereferences freed memory IN THE MAIN PROCESS (crash or memory corruption). context_non_venue.why: FOURTH independent application-level case study, and the strongest single piece of evidence so far that this class is SYSTEMATICALLY DISCOVERABLE rather than incidental. DbGate (dbgate/dbgate) is a database-management GUI whose desktop build is Electron. Read end-to-end from the GHSA page. THE CHAIN, verbatim from the advisory: (1) STORED SINK — `packages/web/src/icons/FontIcon.svelte` treats any icon string starting with ``. This makes `applicationIcon` a stored XSS sink. (2) PRIVILEGE — `app/src/electron.js` sets `nodeIntegration: true` and `contextIsolation: false`, so 'JavaScript gained through XSS can access Node/Electron APIs, making local code execution possible'. (3) POC — an app-definition JSON whose `applicationIcon` is a benign ``, with `usageRules` regexes set to match any database so the icon is certain to render. WHY THIS MATTERS TO THE ARGUMENT — four defensible uses: (1) SAME REPORTER, THIRD APP. The reporter credited on this advisory is `ngocnn97` — per this repo's own earlier entries, the same reporter as SiYuan's stored-XSS advisory (GHSA-phhp-9rm9-6gr2) and Notesnook's Web Clipper advisory (CVE-2026-33976). One researcher has now landed the identical XSS→RCE technique against THREE unrelated codebases. That is direct evidence the family-(A) pattern is mechanically findable at scale by a human, which is precisely the argument for automating it — the motivating observation a discovery thesis wants. (2) A NEW SINK TYPE: FRAMEWORK RAW-HTML DIRECTIVE. Prior corpus sinks were browser DOM APIs — `insertAdjacentHTML` (SiYuan), `contentDocument.write` and `srcdoc` (Notesnook), `innerHTML` (DeepChat). This one is Svelte's `{@html}`, i.e. a deliberate escape hatch out of a framework's automatic escaping. That generalizes to a compact, greppable predicate across the whole modern-frontend Electron population: `{@html}` (Svelte) / `v-html` (Vue) / `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` (React) reachable from stored data, inside a renderer with `nodeIntegration:true`. A DOM-API-only sink list misses all three. (3) A NEW DELIVERY CHANNEL: THE APP'S OWN CONFIGURATION FILE. The payload does not arrive over the network or via sync — the victim IMPORTS OR SAVES an attacker-supplied application-definition JSON, which DbGate later loads through `apps/get-all-apps`. Together with Notesnook's clip-sync and PDF-export paths this establishes a general point: in desktop apps the untrusted-input frontier includes project/config/profile files, a surface a network-facing web fuzzer never reaches. (4) SAME BUG, TWO SEVERITIES — THE CLEANEST MOTIVATION SENTENCE IN THE CORPUS. DbGate ships the same Svelte code as a web app and as an Electron desktop app, and the advisory scores the two separately: in the web UI the impact is 'token theft, session hijacking, and performing privileged actions as the victim inside DbGate'; in Electron it is local code execution. Identical source, identical sink, and the desktop runtime alone converts a session bug into an RCE. That is the thesis's premise stated by a vendor, in one advisory, without any interpretation needed.

The watch now holds TWELVE vendor-published XSS→RCE advisories across FOUR independent Electron applications: SiYuan x8, Notesnook x2, DeepChat x1, DbGate x1.
